1058.title: Holding history lightly
1058.hook: pride and grievance both can weigh down
1058.howItsDone: Muslim teachers point to Qur'an 2:134 and 49:13 when warning against boasting about ancestors or living in old grievances, and to the Prophet's forgiveness at the opening of Mecca as a model of setting old scores down.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aisha's answer about khuluq. Your line was his character was the qur'an.

Two backpacks. One is stuffed with trophies: the great libraries, the domes, the astronomers, the poets, the cities scholars crossed deserts to reach. The other is stuffed with stones: the sieges, the conquests, the colonial years, the old wrongs nobody ever answered for. This year has handed out both bags. Some people carry only the first, some only the second, and either one, carried long enough, bends the back. So what do you do with a history that heavy?
screen: `A BAG OF TROPHIES.` → `A BAG OF STONES.` → `EITHER ONE BENDS THE BACK.`

segments.voice: First, a verse that can sound almost cold. Speaking of the prophets and their families who came before, the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Those are a people who have passed away. Theirs is that which they earned, and yours is that which ye earn. And ye will not be asked of what they used to do." Some readers hear it as lifting a weight: nobody is credited with an earlier generation's glories, and nobody is charged with its sins. Each person's own account is the one that's open. Second, the trophies. The Qur'an cuts pride in ancestry down to size: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." By that measure, a golden age is something to learn from and give thanks for, not a badge anyone inherits. Third, the stones. Grievance can be just; real wrongs were done, and the Qur'an doesn't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. But it also warns against letting old hatred bend present judgment. Pickthall again: "let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty." The wrong is remembered; it just doesn't get to write the next sentence. Fourth, a picture from the seerah. When the Prophet ﷺ entered Mecca, the city that had driven him out, the sources describe a general pardon for its people instead of a settling of scores. He carried it, and he set it down. Lightly doesn't mean forgetting. It means carrying history in your hands, where you can look at it, instead of on your back, where it bends you.
screen: `THEIRS IS THAT WHICH THEY EARNED.` · `THE NOBLEST: THE BEST IN CONDUCT.` · `LET NOT HATRED BEND YOUR JUSTICE.` · `MECCA: HE SET THE OLD SCORE DOWN.` · then, large: `YOURS IS THAT WHICH YE EARN.`

segments.voice: Find one old resentment: something done to you, to your family, or to people like you. You don't have to decide it was fine; just hold it in your hands instead of on your back, name it as you breathe in, and let your hands open a little as you breathe out. If you pray, you can ask Allah for justice where it's owed and lightness for your own heart; if you don't, simply notice whether the weight shifts.
Seerah, the biography of the Prophet's life, where Mecca's conquest is remembered for a pardon instead of a settling of scores. Today's word.
Your line: carry it lightly. Remembered, but not worn like a weight. Day one thousand fifty-eight, done.

1059.title: What will you leave?
1059.hook: a well, a book, a child's prayer
1059.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqa jariya in forms such as funding wells, mosques, schools, copies of the Qur'an or trees, often on behalf of parents who have died, and children make du'a for their parents after prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two backpacks, trophies and stones, and the seerah's pardon at Mecca. Your line was carry it lightly.

A well, dug in hot ground, still giving water long after the man who paid for it is gone. A book, copied and recopied, still read by people who will never meet its author. A child, grown now, raising her hands after the prayer to ask mercy for a parent who died years ago. None of them is a building with a name on it, or a fortune, or a title. Yet a saying of the Prophet ﷺ names exactly these three as the things that keep working after a life ends.
screen: `A WELL, STILL GIVING WATER.` → `A BOOK, STILL BEING READ.` → `A CHILD, STILL PRAYING.`

segments.voice: First, the saying itself. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: a charity that keeps on flowing, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. Three doors left open after the house is closed. Second, the flowing charity. Its Arabic name is sadaqa jariya. Abu Dawud keeps a story about a companion, Sa'd ibn Ubada, whose mother had died. He asked the Prophet which charity was best, and the answer was water. So Sa'd dug a well and said it was for his mother. A report in Tirmidhi also tells of a well in Medina that Uthman bought so people could draw from it freely. Water, given once, keeps giving. Third, the knowledge. This whole year has been full of it: scholars who wrote, teachers who taught a single student who taught another. A lesson passed on keeps working in someone else's life, whether or not anyone remembers who taught it first. Fourth, the child's prayer: in the hadith's words, a righteous child who prays for the parent, a son or a daughter asking mercy by name after the prayer. Then notice what's missing from the list: wealth and power. A well can be a share in one. Knowledge can be one skill taught well. And the Qur'an widens the frame, in a verse that speaks of a record of what people sent ahead and the traces they left behind.
screen: `WHEN A PERSON DIES, THREE THINGS GO ON.` · `SADAQA JARIYA: CHARITY THAT RUNS LIKE WATER.` · `KNOWLEDGE THAT KEEPS ON WORKING.` · `A RIGHTEOUS CHILD WHO PRAYS FOR THEM.` · then, large: `WHAT THEY SENT AHEAD, AND THE TRACES THEY LEFT.`

segments.voice: Look at the three doors: something that keeps giving, like water, a book for a library, a tree, a scholarship or a ramp; one thing you know that someone younger needs, a recipe, a skill, how to pray, how to fix a bike; or a child in your life you could be more present for. Choose one door and picture the smallest first step. If you pray, you can ask Allah to accept it; if not, simply hold the plan.
Sadaqa jariya, a flowing charity like a well that keeps giving water long after the person who paid for it is gone. Today's word.
Your line: three doors left open. None of them needs a fortune. That's day one thousand fifty-nine.

1060.title: The chain back to him
1060.hook: every Muslim alive learned from someone, back to the companions
1060.tomorrow: Year three close: the long story
1060.howItsDone: Hadith are studied with their chains of narrators, and Qur'an recitation is traditionally learned face to face with a teacher; some receive an ijaza, a permission to teach that names the teachers before them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a well, a book and a child's prayer: sadaqa jariya. Your line was three doors left open.

Who taught you to tie your shoes? The name may be gone already. Try another: who taught you the first prayer you knew, or the first verse, or the first words of a language you love? Sometimes that name comes back. Now ask who taught them, and who taught that person. For the Qur'an and the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ, Muslims say the thread doesn't vanish into fog. It runs back, teacher before teacher, to the companions who heard him. Each person along it is one link.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU?` → `AND WHO TAUGHT THEM?` → `BACK TO THE COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Open a hadith collection and the reports begin with names: so-and-so told us that so-and-so told him, that so-and-so heard the Prophet say. That list of names is the isnad, the chain a saying leans on. Scholars weighed each link: was this person honest, careful, did they actually meet the one they quote? Second, why it mattered. In the introduction to Sahih Muslim, the scholar Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak is quoted saying, in effect, that the isnad is part of the religion, and without it anyone could say whatever they liked. The chain was a guard against invention. Third, the chain is people, not paper. Qur'an recitation is still taught face to face, the student reading to a teacher who listens and corrects, and some receive a written permission, an ijaza, that lists their teachers, and their teachers' teachers. Fourth, how the chain grows. The Prophet said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: convey from me, even a single verse. And in another hadith there: the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Learning is only half of it. The isnad itself names particular transmitters, weighed one by one. But the command to convey asks for as little as one verse, and the same habit of passing on runs through lives no chain records: a mother teaching a du'a, a neighbor showing a new Muslim how to make wudu, a teacher who stayed late. Everything this year has told was carried this way. Not by a book alone, but by a chain of people.
screen: `ISNAD: SO-AND-SO TOLD US THAT…` · `A GUARD AGAINST INVENTION.` · `IJAZA: A LIST OF TEACHERS IN YOUR HAND.` · `CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.` · then, large: `LEARN THE QUR'AN AND TEACH IT.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you know by heart, a verse, a du'a, a recipe, a line of advice, and say it to yourself once, slowly. Then ask whose voice you first heard it in: that person is your link, and if you can, go one step further back to where they got it. If you pray, you can make du'a for that teacher, living or gone; if not, simply hold a quiet thank-you for them.
Isnad, the chain of narrators a hadith leans on, teacher before teacher, back to the companions who heard the Prophet himself. Today's word.
Your line: a chain of people. What you know came to you through someone. See you tomorrow, for the last day of year three.

1061.title: Year three close: the long story
1061.hook: from the cave of Hira to your nearest mosque, fourteen centuries of people
1061.carry: you are in the story now
1061.howItsDone: Muslims often make du'a for those who came before them in faith, using words like Qur'an 59:10, and many keep alive the names of the Prophet's companions and the scholars who followed by reading their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the isnad, and your line: a chain of people. Today, the last day of year three.

Read. Tradition says that word came to a man alone in the dark, in a cave on a mountain above Mecca, and would not let him go. Now, a mosque on an ordinary street near you. Shoes in a rack by the door. A child running between the rows before the prayer starts. An older man folding a prayer mat. Between that cave and this doorway lie century after century of people, and this year has tried to meet them. Before a new year opens, a look back down the road.
screen: `A CAVE ABOVE MECCA: READ.` → `A MOSQUE ON YOUR STREET.` → `CENTURY AFTER CENTURY OF PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: On the first day of this year, your line was: people carried it. Here is who carried it. First, the Prophet ﷺ himself, in full. Mecca before the revelation. The orphan, the trader, Khadijah's husband. The cave, and the command that came there, in Pickthall's translation: "Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth." The years of persecution, the sorrow, Ta'if, the night journey, the road to Yathrib, and Medina. Second, those who walked beside him. The first circle. The mothers of the believers. His family. The freed slave who called the prayer, the women who asked hard questions. Third, the hard chapter. The succession, the caliphs, the first split, and Karbala, told with Sunni and Shia memory side by side, neither one ranked. Fourth, the long road after. Damascus and Baghdad, al-Andalus and Cairo, Timbuktu and Samarkand, Istanbul, Isfahan, Delhi, Java, China. Scholars, poets, builders, rulers who were merciful and rulers who failed. The modern centuries, the houses of prayer, the holy days, kept across all of it. And these last days drew the lessons: unity builds, knowledge as worship, ordinary hands, mercy remembered, failures admitted, women who were there, many faces, the prayer that went on, back to the source, his character, history held lightly, what you'll leave, and the chain. Whatever brought you here, faith, curiosity, a partner, a parent, you have now heard the long story, and in the loose sense of yesterday's chain, whoever hears a story and passes some of it on becomes part of it.
screen: `FIRST: THE PROPHET, IN FULL.` · `THOSE WHO WALKED BESIDE HIM.` · `THE SPLIT, TOLD WITHOUT RANKING.` · `THE LONG ROAD, CITY BY CITY.` · then, large: `READ: IN THE NAME OF THY LORD WHO CREATETH.`

segments.voice: Bring back a few faces from this year: Khadijah, Bilal, Fatima, Husayn, a scholar in Baghdad, a woman who founded a school, a grandmother you'll never know by name. In the Qur'an, later believers are described praying for those before them, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith." If you pray, you can say that line for all of them; if not, simply hold the long line of people in your mind.
Karbala, the hard chapter of the succession and the first split, remembered with Sunni and Shia memory side by side. Today's word.
Your line: you are in the story now. Year three, done; tomorrow, year four asks how and why.

1062.title: How, and why
1062.hook: years one to three told the story, and this year asks how Muslims live it and think it through
1062.howItsDone: Muslims learn how to practice from parents, imams and teachers, and some bring their questions to a scholar or a study circle; the report of Jibril's visit can be taught as a summary of the whole religion, told through questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three closed, and your line was: you are in the story now. Which name did you write down to carry forward? Today, a new year opens. Day one thousand sixty-two.

Medina, a gathering already under way. A stranger walks in, his clothes startling white, his hair very black, and no dust of travel on him, though nobody there knows who he is. He sits down in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, close, knee to knee, and starts asking questions. What is Islam? What is faith? What is it to do good? The Prophet answers each one. Then the man goes. Later the Prophet tells his companions who it was: the angel Jibril, come to teach them their religion. Notice how he taught it. With questions.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE, KNEE TO KNEE.`

segments.voice: That report is recorded in Sahih Muslim, and it gives this year its shape. The first three years told the story: the Qur'an's words, the Prophet's life, the people and the centuries after. Year four turns from what happened to how. How do Muslims actually live this? How do they pray, fast, give, travel to Mecca? And why: why these words, why this order, why do scholars sometimes disagree? First, the plan: the pillars, taken slowly, one by one, starting tomorrow with the testimony. After that come the ways of thinking that grew around them: how reports of the Prophet are judged, law and its schools, belief, the inner life, and the shape of a life from birth to death. Second, the questions are welcome. The Qur'an tells its first hearers, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Asking is part of how the religion gets handed on. Even the Prophet is told to keep asking for more: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Third, how sits next to why. A person can learn the movements of the prayer in an afternoon. The why behind them can take a lifetime. The Jibril report itself keeps the two side by side: islam, the doing, and faith, the inner yes, asked about one after the other. Fourth, this year describes; it doesn't decide. Where Sunni and Shia Muslims practice differently, or the schools of law part ways, you'll hear who says what, plainly, and nobody ranked. So the question you walk in with matters. Somebody who has prayed for decades and somebody who has never seen a prayer mat can both bring one.

The practice: three questions. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Then let questions come about how Muslims live, or why they do what they do. Maybe it's a small one: why do people take their shoes off at the door of a mosque? Maybe a big one: what does it mean to say God is one? Don't answer them. Just catch three. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words. When the bell ends, write the three down somewhere you'll find them this year. The bell holds the time.
How. The question this year keeps asking: how Muslims live their faith, and, right beside it, why. Today's word.
Your line: bring your questions. Today, ask one of your three out loud, to a friend, a teacher, or a book, and see what comes back. Tomorrow, two sentences. Day one thousand sixty-two.

1063.title: Two sentences
1063.hook: I testify there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger
1063.howItsDone: Muslims hear the shahadah in every call to prayer and recite it while sitting in the ritual prayer; some say it on waking and before sleep, and it is the declaration a person makes on becoming Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger in white who taught by asking, and your line: bring your questions. Did you ask one out loud? Today the pillars begin. Day one thousand sixty-three.

Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. If you've ever stood near a mosque at prayer time, you may have heard those words carried over the rooftops in the call to prayer. In English: I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is His messenger. Two sentences. Said in a breath or two. And Muslims place them first among the pillars of their faith, the testimony, the shahadah. This block of the year takes the pillars slowly, and the days ahead stay with these two sentences alone.

Start with the verb they both begin with. Not I think, not I feel. I testify. I bear witness. It's a witness's word, the word for someone who has seen something and will say so in front of others. It turns a belief into a statement made out loud, with your name on it. And in the Qur'an, the first one to testify isn't a person at all. Pickthall's translation of surah three: "Allah (Himself) is witness that there is no God save Him. And the angels and the men of learning (too are witness)." So a Muslim saying the shahadah joins a line of witnesses that, in the Qur'an's picture, begins with God. Next, the first sentence. It's about God: there is no god but Allah. A no, then a yes. We'll spend a day on each half. Then the second sentence, about a person: Muhammad is His messenger. It answers a question the first one leaves open. If there is one God, how do people know how to live toward Him? Through the messenger, who brought the message and showed it. Last, where the two sentences live. In the call to prayer, out loud, several times a day. Inside the prayer itself, said quietly while sitting. Whispered by people at the end of their lives. And said by someone becoming Muslim, which is a day of its own later this week. Short enough for a child to learn. Deep enough for a lifetime of asking what each word means. That is why Muslims can say two sentences hold it all.
screen: `ONE ABOUT GOD, ONE ABOUT A PERSON.`
`IN THE CALL, THE PRAYER, THE LAST BREATH.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it slowly, meaning each word. Settle, and breathe. If you're Muslim, say the shahadah once, at half your usual speed, and stop on each word long enough to mean it: I testify. No god. But Allah. Muhammad. His messenger. If you're not Muslim, you can simply listen to the words in your mind, as the words Muslims say, and notice which one you'd most like to ask about. Either way, let the last word fade, and sit in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Shahadah. The testimony: two sentences that bear witness to one God and His messenger. Today's word.

Your line: two sentences hold it all. Today, listen for the shahadah once, in a recording of the call to prayer, or in your own voice. Tomorrow, the first word of it: no. Day one thousand sixty-three.

1064.title: "No god"
1064.hook: the shahada starts with a no: clearing away everything worshiped besides God
1064.howItsDone: Muslims say la ilaha illallah in prayer and in remembrance, and some teachers explain its opening negation as setting aside anything that competes with God, from idols to money, fame or desire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shahadah, and your line: two sentences hold it all. Did you hear them once, in a call to prayer or your own voice? Today, the first word that clears the ground. Day one thousand sixty-four.

A night sky, in a story the Qur'an tells about Abraham. He sees a star and says, this is my Lord. The star sets. Then the moon rises, bright, and he says it again. The moon sets. Then the sun, the biggest yet, and the sun goes down too. And Abraham says, in Pickthall's translation: "I love not things that set." Before he could turn to the one he called the Creator of the heavens and the earth, he had to let go of everything that rises and falls. The shahadah opens in the same order.

La ilaha. No god. The testimony doesn't start with a yes. It starts by clearing the ground. First, the word itself. La is no. Ilah is a god in the widest sense: whatever is worshiped, whatever a person serves, the thing they give themselves to. So la ilaha is a sweeping no: nothing deserves that. Second, what counts as a god. In Abraham's day, and in Mecca in the Prophet's day, people bowed to idols of stone and wood. But the Qur'an widens the word on purpose. Pickthall's translation asks: "Hast thou seen him who chooseth for his god his own lust?" A god there isn't a statue. It's a want that runs a life. Some Muslim teachers read this as a warning that money, status, fear, or someone's approval can quietly take that place. Third, why the no comes first. A yes added to a crowded shelf just becomes one more thing on the shelf. Clearing comes before choosing. Abraham watched the star, the moon and the sun go down before he turned his face elsewhere. Fourth, read this way, the no is not a sour word. It frees. If nothing that sets deserves your whole self, then the boss, the screen, the bank balance and the crowd can be important without being in charge. And it lands on this week's turning point. A few days ago this path closed year three, the long story of people. Now year four begins inside one sentence, and that sentence begins by telling every smaller master: not you.
screen: `A GOD CAN BE A WANT THAT RUNS A LIFE.`
`A NO THAT SETS A PERSON FREE.`

segments.voice: The practice: name one thing you over-serve. Settle, and let your breath slow. Ask yourself, honestly and without scolding, what gets more of you than it deserves. Your phone, someone's opinion, work, worry, a craving. Don't fight it. Just name it, quietly, the way Abraham named the star. Then let it set, like the star did, and rest in the space it leaves for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can say la ilaha slowly as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
No god. La ilaha: the shahadah's first move, a no to everything that rises and sets. Today's word.
Your line: first, no. Today, when the thing you named tugs at you, give it one small no and notice what happens. Tomorrow, after the no, the yes. Day one thousand sixty-four.
